items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary for Patient 2:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Gender: Male
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]
Diagnosis: An abnormal opening between the food pipe and a blood vessel, causing the patient to vomit large amounts of blood; a 6 cm balloon-like bulge in the main blood vessel in the chest, located just past the artery that supplies the left arm

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 48-year-old male with a history of high blood pressure. Three years ago, he had a procedure where small mesh tubes were placed in his heart arteries to keep them open. He came to the emergency room after vomiting a large amount of blood. Doctors used a camera to look inside his food pipe. They found a large sore with a red spot in the middle part of the food pipe. They also found a small pouch at the lower end of the sore. Scans showed a 6 cm balloon-like bulge in the main chest blood vessel. This bulge was wearing through into the food pipe.

The patient had surgery through a cut in the back and side of the chest. Doctors replaced the bulging part of the blood vessel with a fabric tube. They saved as many small blood vessels between the ribs as they could. They tied off the others with stitches. Doctors cleaned the opening between the food pipe and blood vessel. They closed it with stitches. They covered the repair with a piece of muscle from between the ribs that still had its blood supply. After surgery, the patient received strong medicines to fight infection.

After surgery, the patient recovered well without any problems. Doctors safely took him off the machine that was helping his blood flow. They made two new openings, one into his stomach and one into his small intestine, for feeding. The patient was sent home. He was told to see his regular doctor and his surgeon for long-term care.

Discharge Medications: None

Instructions: No heavy lifting, straining, or hard physical activity for the next 6 to 8 weeks. Follow-up visits were set up with the regular doctor and surgeon.

Condition at Discharge: Stable

Patient Name: [redacted]
Medical Record Number: [redacted]
Gender: Female
Age: 67 years

Hospital Course:
The 67-year-old female patient had a stage 3 hole in the macula, the central part of the eye. She came to the hospital on [redacted] because her left eye vision had gotten worse over the past month. The patient had eye surgery to remove the gel inside the eye and peel a thin layer from the retina. A special dye was used to help the surgeon see better. Gas was put in the eye to help it heal. Eye scans taken four weeks after surgery showed the light-sensing layer was still damaged over a wide area. The patient could see 20/100, which means her vision was still limited. At six weeks, the retina had pulled away from the back of the eye in some areas, but not the central vision area. There were several tears in the retina. She had another eye surgery to fix the detached retina. Laser treatment was used to seal the tears. Gas was again put in the eye. At six months, the patient could see 20/40. Eye scans showed the light-sensing layer was healing in many areas of the macula. There was still some damage under the very center of the macula. By one year, the patient could see 20/25, which is close to normal. Eye scans showed the light-sensing layer in the center of the macula had fully healed.

Diagnosis:
Stage 3 hole in the macula. Detached retina with several tears, but the central vision area was not affected.

Treatment:
Eye surgery to remove the gel inside the eye. Peeling of a thin layer from the retina using a special dye. Gas placed in the eye to help healing. Laser treatment to seal retina tears.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient has gotten much better. Her vision improved to 20/25, which is close to normal. The light-sensing layer in the center of the macula has fully healed.

Follow-up Care:
The patient will need regular check-ups to watch her vision and the health of her retina.

items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Name]
Age: 61
Gender: Female
Admitted: [Admission Date]
Discharged: [Discharge Date]
Diagnosis: A bulge in the artery behind the knee that caused damage to a nerve controlling the foot

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the emergency room with swelling in the right knee and calf. The patient had severe pain in the right leg and weakness when trying to lift the right foot upward. Doctors found that a nerve near the knee was damaged, causing the foot to drop down. A special brace was put on the foot right away. More tests showed a bulge in the blood vessel behind the knee. This was fixed by placing a small tube inside the blood vessel to keep it open. The patient stayed in the hospital for 2 weeks before going home. At a checkup 6 months later, the patient had no pain or swelling. However, the patient still could not lift the right foot normally. Blood flow to the foot was normal.

Follow-Up Instructions:
The patient should keep seeing the blood vessel surgeon for any remaining problems. The patient should have regular tests to check the blood vessels. The patient should see a physical therapist for help with the foot drop. The physical therapist will give exercises to do at home.

Patient summary:

Ms. X is a 62-year-old woman who came to the hospital with noisy breathing, trouble breathing during activity, and a dry cough. A physical exam found a hard lump in her thyroid gland and swollen lymph nodes on the same side of her neck. A test using a small needle to collect cells showed thyroid cancer. A CT scan showed the cancer had spread into the thyroid gland and a large mass on the right side of her neck. The patient had surgery to remove the entire thyroid gland and lymph nodes on the right side of the neck. The surgery showed the cancer had grown into the windpipe. A blood clot made of cancer cells was found during surgery and was easily removed. Lab tests on the tissue showed two types of thyroid cancer, one fast-growing and one slower-growing. The patient then received radiation treatment using a pill and a machine that aimed beams at the neck. Sixteen months later, the patient is alive and doing well with no signs that the cancer has come back or spread to other parts of the body.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 45-year-old woman who had been pregnant twice, was admitted in April 2018. She had cancer of the lining of the uterus, high grade. A small tissue sample from the uterus confirmed the diagnosis. The patient had family members on her mothers side who had cancer of the female organs. A special scan showed a tumor about 1.5 inches wide in the upper part of the uterus. The tumor had grown through the wall of the uterus and spread past the left tube that connects the ovary to the uterus. Another type of scan showed the cancer may have spread to lymph nodes in the belly area. Lab tests on the tumor showed it had certain features that might make it respond well to a specific treatment.

Treatment:
The patient received a medicine called pembrolizumab through a vein every 3 weeks. After three treatments, the tumor in the uterus went away completely. To check how well the treatment worked, doctors did surgery using small cuts in the belly. They removed the uterus, lymph nodes from the pelvis and belly area, a fatty tissue layer, and checked the belly cavity. No cancer could be seen during surgery. Tests showed the cancer had gone away in the uterus, cervix, left ovary, and nearby tissue. Doctors removed 41 lymph nodes. One lymph node in the right pelvis had a tiny spot of cancer. One lymph node in the belly area had a small cluster of cancer cells that showed signs of shrinking.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has gone 24 months with no signs that the cancer has grown or come back. The patient had no bad reactions to treatment. The patient was sent to a specialist to check her risk for inherited conditions. A change was found in a gene called MLH1. Experts are not sure if this gene change causes health problems.

Hospital Stay Summary

Patient: 40-year-old female with chest pain

Admission Date: [Date of Admission]
Discharge Date: [Date of Discharge]

Reason for Admission:
The patient came to the hospital with severe, squeezing chest pain in the center of her chest. The pain lasted three hours. It got worse with physical activity and felt better with rest.

Hospital Stay:
When the patient arrived, her heart rate and blood pressure were normal. The physical exam showed no other problems. Blood tests for basic health markers came back normal. But a test for heart damage showed high levels at 11.3 ng/ml.

A heart rhythm test showed changes that meant the patient was having a serious heart attack. The patient was given medicines including aspirin, a heart rate medicine, a cholesterol medicine, and a blood thinner through an IV.

The first hospital could not do a heart procedure, so the patient was moved to our hospital. Doctors used a thin tube to look at the heart arteries. The test showed the main heart arteries looked normal and open.

Within 24 hours, the patient had severe chest pain again. Another heart rhythm test showed new signs of heart damage. The heart damage test went up to more than 40 ng/ml.

Doctors did another heart artery test right away. They found a tear in the wall of a main heart artery. A smaller branch artery was fully blocked. This was caused by a tear that happened on its own in the artery wall. The patient was given two blood-thinning medicines, aspirin and clopidogrel. She also stayed on the cholesterol and heart rate medicines.

Over the next 48 hours, the patient was watched closely in the intensive care unit. Her chest pain went away. Her heart rate and blood pressure stayed normal. Another heart artery test showed the tear in the main artery had healed on its own. The blocked smaller artery now showed a long tear along the wall. This confirmed the artery tear happened on its own.

More tests showed the patient has a condition where artery walls do not form normally. The patient was kept on medicines and watched closely for one year. During this time, she had no symptoms. The patient was sent home on [Date of Discharge] in good health.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

PATIENT INFORMATION:

Name: [Patient Name]
Age: 65 years
Gender: Male
Admission Date: [Admission Date]
Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]
Reason for Admission: Painful growth at right lower back tooth area

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient came to our hospital because of a painful growth in the right lower back tooth area. The patient shared that he has been chewing pan for the past fifteen years. He chews about 3-5 packets per day. During the exam, doctors found a hard, painful growth about 4 by 3 cm in size. The growth was on the gum ridge where teeth 45 and 46 used to be. It spread into the jawbone and the inside of the right cheek. The edges of the growth were raised and the base felt hard when touched. Doctors also felt a firm lump about 3 by 2 cm under the right side of the jaw.

Doctors believed the growth was cancer affecting the right jawbone and cheek area near teeth 45 and 46. A special scan with dye was done to see inside the body. The scan showed a cancerous mass that had spread to nearby lymph nodes. A small tissue sample was taken and tested. The test confirmed the growth was a type of skin cancer called squamous cell carcinoma. It was a slow-growing type. Based on how far the cancer has spread, it was rated as stage IVA-T4a N1 M0. This means it is advanced but has not spread to distant body parts.

TREATMENT:

Doctors recommended surgery to remove the cancerous growth. The patient chose not to have the surgery. Because of how advanced the cancer is and the patient's choice, he was sent to a comfort care team. This team will help manage his pain and other symptoms.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:

Slow-growing skin cancer of the right jawbone and cheek area near teeth 45 and 46. The cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes.

RECOMMENDATIONS:

The patient should see his cancer doctor regularly for help with pain and symptoms. The patient should stop using pan and all tobacco products. The patient learned why eating healthy foods and living a healthy lifestyle matters when dealing with cancer.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:

None

FOLLOW-UP:

The patient has an appointment with his cancer doctor in two weeks. The patient should call the hospital if any new symptoms appear or current symptoms get worse. The patient's medical records have been sent to his cancer doctor for continued care.

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was hospitalized for severe back pain and trouble breathing after a back injury. The patient was crushed against a broken concrete block. X-rays showed a break and collapse in the lower back bone called T12. The patient was diagnosed with a broken and shifted T12 bone, several broken ribs, and blood and air trapped around the right lung.

Treatment Provided:
The patient had spine surgery to connect the bones from T10 to L2 using metal rods and screws. Bone from the patient's own body was used to help the bones heal together. This surgery helped the patient sit up sooner and breathe better. The surgery went well.

Postoperative Course:
Three hours after surgery, the patient had pain in the lower legs and back. The patient also had trouble moving the lower legs. A scan was done right away. It showed no bone pieces pressing into the spinal canal at T12. Doctors found that blood had collected near the spine after surgery. The patient needed a second surgery right away. During this surgery, doctors removed parts of two back bones called T11 and T12. They found and removed a large blood clot.

Discharge Condition and Plan:
The patient slowly got better over time. Six months after the second surgery, the patient could move normally again. However, the patient still had pain from light touch and needed medicine for this. The patient was able to walk with a cane on day 20. The patient went home on day 28.

Medications and Follow-up:
The patient's medicines and follow-up plan will be discussed at a follow-up visit.

Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with a broken and shifted T12 bone, several broken ribs, and blood and air trapped around the right lung. The patient had spine surgery, but blood collected near the spine afterward. A second surgery was needed to remove the blood clot. The patient is a 69-year-old white man with a history of schizophrenia. He was admitted to our facility because he was not moving normally and was confused. The patient had come from a mental health hospital. There, he was on strong older medicines for mental illness called fluphenazine and haloperidol. These medicines made his restlessness and behavior problems worse. He was then started on another medicine called chlorpromazine before coming to our facility.

When the patient arrived at our facility, he was taken off the mental illness medicines. He was given lorazepam through an IV to help with his symptoms. During his stay, his movement problems came and went. He also had a fast heart rate, heavy sweating, and made humming sounds. The patient had very stiff arms and legs. His limbs would stay in any position they were placed in. He would resist being moved and would also follow commands without thinking. A test that checks brain waves was done during the stay. It only showed faster brain activity because of the high doses of lorazepam he was getting.

The patient had three sessions of a treatment that uses small electrical currents to help the brain. This treatment had no problems and helped him get better. He was then started on a medicine called amantadine to help with his movement problems. The patient also had a bladder infection that was treated with medicines to kill germs. Treating this infection helped clear up his confusion.

Near the end of the hospital stay, the patient slowly got better from his movement problems. His blood test results went back to normal. The patient waited three weeks before starting a new medicine called clozapine. This medicine was slowly increased without causing a dangerous reaction to mental illness medicines or movement problems coming back. The patient was sent back to the mental health hospital unit after staying for one month.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

This is a discharge summary for a woman in her 50s who has gone through menopause. The patient was found to have breast cancer that had spread to nearby lymph nodes (Stage IIB). The patient received cancer-fighting drugs before surgery. The treatment plan included two types of drug combinations given through an IV. The first combination (EC) was given every 3 weeks, 4 times total. The second combination included three drugs (DOC, pertuzumab, and trastuzumab). During treatment, the patient had some side effects. These included moderate loose stools, mild tiredness, mild swelling, and mild tingling or numbness in the hands and feet. The patient had other health conditions including a mental health condition, high blood sugar, and high cholesterol. All of these were well controlled with medicine. The patient smoked 10 cigarettes a day and drank alcohol sometimes. The patient's liver and kidneys were working normally.

Summary of Treatment:

Several medicines were given to help with side effects. A steroid helped with swelling and pain. A shot helped keep white blood cell counts up. Medicine was given for nausea. An herbal medicine was given for tingling and numbness in the hands and feet. The patient also took a probiotic to prevent loose stools. When loose stools happened, another medicine was used to control them. After the second round of the first drug combination, the patient's blood fat levels went up a little. The levels stayed about the same for a while without any treatment. After the third round of the second drug combination, blood fat levels jumped very high (770 mg/dL). This was a serious increase, but the patient had no symptoms. The fourth round of treatment was still given. A medicine to lower blood fats was started that same day. The patient took 200 mg twice a day. After 16 days, the blood fat level dropped a lot (287 mg/dL). The blood fat medicine was stopped on day 28 of the fourth round. The level went back to normal (212 mg/dL) by day 39.

Course After Chemotherapy:

Surgery was done 39 days after the last round of cancer-fighting drugs. More cancer-fighting drugs (pertuzumab and trastuzumab) were started again 52 days after surgery. Blood fat levels stayed normal during this time. The patient had mildly high liver enzyme levels starting in the second round of EC treatment. These levels stayed about the same until the end of treatment before surgery. No other new medicines were given during treatment.

Diagnosis:

The patient was found to have Stage IIB breast cancer. The cancer cells tested positive for estrogen receptors. The cancer cells tested positive for progesterone receptors. The cancer cells had too much of a protein called HER-2. The cancer cells were also tested for Ki-67, which shows how fast they grow.

Condition at the Time of Discharge:

The patient was in stable condition when leaving the hospital. Blood fat levels had returned to normal (212 mg/dL). The patient did not have any major side effects from the cancer-fighting drugs.

Follow-up Care:

The patient will be watched closely to make sure the breast cancer does not come back. The patient will receive follow-up care based on standard guidelines.

The patient, an 18-year-old man, was admitted to the chest and heart surgery department at Wonju Severance Christian Hospital. He had a swelling on his left arm that pulsed with his heartbeat. The swelling had been there for more than 17 years. During the physical exam, doctors found a pulsing lump on the inner side of his left upper arm. The lump was not painful when touched. It measured about 1.5 inches long and less than 1 inch wide. It was located just above the inner elbow area. An ultrasound using color imaging showed an abnormal connection between the main artery and vein in the arm. Blood was flowing through this connection at a rate of 240 milliliters per minute. A CT scan with dye confirmed there was an abnormal connection between the artery and vein.

The patient had surgery while fully asleep under anesthesia. The surgeon closed the abnormal opening using permanent stitches through the vein side. Six months after surgery, a follow-up CT scan showed the blood vessels looked normal. The patient had no problems such as trouble breathing or poor blood flow to the lower arm. His blood pressure was normal. His lab test results were normal.

The patient was sent home with instructions to see his regular doctor for follow-up. Regular follow-up visits with imaging scans were recommended.

COVID-19 lung infection

Hospital Course:
The patient came to hospital 1 with fever, trouble breathing during activity, and upset stomach with vomiting. Blood tests showed a normal white blood cell count of 7.85x103/uL but very low infection-fighting cells. Chest scans showed hazy patches in both lungs. A nose swab test confirmed the patient had COVID-19. The patient received antibiotics called ceftriaxone and azithromycin. He also received hydroxychloroquine, vitamin C pills, and zinc pills for six days.
On day 3, the patient could not breathe on his own. A breathing tube was placed and a machine helped him breathe. On day 13, he moved to hospital 2, which had a special blood oxygen machine called ECMO. Doctors connected this machine to blood vessels in his leg and neck right away. The patient was kept asleep with medicine and given muscle relaxers. He received a five-day course of a steroid called dexamethasone. Blood thinners were given through an IV to prevent clots. First heparin was used, then bivalirudin. While on the ECMO machine, the patient slowly got better. Doctors were able to lower the machine settings over time. On day 75, the patient no longer needed the breathing machine. He was sent to a rehab center to continue getting better.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient came to hospital 1 with a COVID-19 lung infection. The nose swab test confirmed this. The patient could not breathe on his own and needed a breathing machine. He moved to hospital 2 for the special blood oxygen machine called ECMO. He made good progress during his stay. The patient no longer needed the breathing machine and was sent to a rehab center.

Henoch-Schonlein Purpura (HSP), a condition that causes inflammation in small blood vessels

Medical History:
History of surgery to remove hemorrhoids

Hospital Course Summary:
On admission, the patient had belly pain, blood in the stool, and a skin rash. Blood tests showed a high white blood cell count, high infection-fighting cells, high platelet count, and high liver enzyme levels. An ultrasound of the belly showed blocked bile flow and gallbladder swelling. CT scans showed thickening of the small intestine wall, fluid around the heart, fluid in the pelvis, and swollen lymph nodes in the belly. The patient was diagnosed with HSP based on official guidelines from European medical groups.

On February 13, 2019, the patient had a faster heart rate and passed dark red bloody stool twice. The total amount was about 400 mL. Blood tests showed a high white blood cell count and high infection-fighting cells. Because of bleeding in the gut, steroid treatment was started. The patient first received medicines to stop bleeding and protect the stomach. Then the patient received antibiotics, calcium, and a protein supplement. A steroid medicine called methylprednisolone was also given twice a day.

By February 15, 2019, the patient's belly pain got better and heart rate returned to normal at about 80 beats per minute. However, the patient still had blood in the stool from time to time. By February 19, 2019, the patient's belly pain and bloody stool stopped. Several medicines were prescribed, and the steroid dose was slowly lowered.

However, the patient came back to the hospital on March 13, 2019, because the pain returned. Blood tests showed a high white blood cell count and high infection-fighting cells. Steroid medicine and a stomach-protecting medicine were given through the vein to help with symptoms. The patient got better by April 1, 2019.

On April 2, 2019, the patient left the hospital. The patient was told to slowly lower the dose of the steroid pill. A follow-up visit was scheduled to check on the patient's health.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was told to keep taking the steroid pill as directed and to slowly lower the dose over time.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [redacted], Age: 59, Gender: Male, Chief Complaint: Heart failure symptoms.

Hospital Course:
The patient was seen at the outpatient clinic. He had heart failure symptoms for 3 weeks. The patient was a smoker and had high blood pressure. He was taking blood pressure medicine that helps relax blood vessels. The patient had an ultrasound of his heart. He also had a test where dye was put into his heart arteries. He had a special scan to look at his heart muscle in detail.

Diagnostic Findings:
The heart ultrasound showed the main pumping chamber was enlarged. The heart was only pumping 22% of its blood with each beat, which is very weak. The heart muscle was not squeezing well overall. The artery test showed severe blockages in all three main heart arteries. The special scan showed a small amount of scarring in parts of the heart wall. Less than 10% of the middle front and bottom walls had scars. The heart wall thickness was normal. A stress test using medicine showed the heart muscle could still work better with more blood flow.

Treatment Approach:
The scan and stress test showed that parts of the heart muscle were still alive. Because of this, the patient was sent for heart bypass surgery to restore blood flow.

Outcome:
A heart ultrasound one year later showed the heart had gotten smaller. The heart was also pumping better than before.

Final Diagnosis:
Severe blockages in all three main heart arteries. Small amount of scarring in less than 10% of the middle front and bottom heart walls. Heart muscle that can still recover with better blood flow.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should keep taking all medicines as directed. The patient should see his regular doctor for ongoing care of his heart disease. The patient should stop smoking.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course:
The patient is a 61-year-old man with mouth cancer. He had surgery for early-stage cancer in 2011. He came back after not seeing doctors for over 4 years. He now had swollen lymph nodes in his neck and left armpit. A small tissue sample showed the cancer had spread to these lymph nodes. The patient joined a research study. He received three cancer drugs called carboplatin, 5-FU, and pembrolizumab at a dose of 200 mg. After 4 rounds of treatment, the cancer showed some shrinking. However, he came in feeling very tired and had low blood pressure with the top number at 70. Doctors found that his immune treatment caused his adrenal glands to stop working properly. These glands sit above the kidneys and make important hormones. He was given a strong steroid medicine called dexamethasone. Later, he switched to another steroid called hydrocortisone. A scan of his brain showed no swelling near the pituitary gland. The scan also showed no cancer spread to the brain. His tiredness went away after ten days. He then started taking pembrolizumab again. The patient continues to take hydrocortisone.

A physical exam showed white flaky skin spread across the scalp. The soles of the feet had thick, widespread flaky skin. The mouth and nails looked normal.

Treatment:
The discharge summary does not contain any information about the patient's treatment plan.

Follow-up:
The patient will see her healthcare provider for care of her LPP.

Disposition:
The patient was sent home. The patient was told to keep seeing her healthcare provider.

Follow-up
The patient was told to come back every six months. This will help check the gum condition and watch for more bone loss.

Final Diagnosis
Based on the exam findings, the patient was diagnosed with serious long-term gum disease. The teeth were loose because the bone holding them had worn away. The thick skin on the palms and soles was caused by a skin condition. This came with excessive sweating.

Discharge Condition
The patient went home in stable condition with care instructions.

Patient Information:
Name: [patient's name]
Age: 50
Gender: Female
Admission Date: [date of admission]
Discharge Date: [date of discharge]
Diagnosis: HDR Syndrome

Hospital Course:
[Patient's name] was admitted to the hospital for treatment of low parathyroid hormone levels. The parathyroid is a small gland in the neck that controls calcium in the blood. At age 33, the patient had a seizure and passed out. After that, doctors found the parathyroid gland was not working well. The cause was unknown at that time. Blood tests showed very low calcium and high phosphorus levels. The parathyroid hormone level was also low. The patient started taking calcium lactate and a form of vitamin D called 1α-hydroxyvitamin D3. These medicines worked well to keep calcium levels normal.

Clinical Findings:
A scan of the head showed heavy calcium buildup in the brain. A scan of the belly showed the right kidney did not form the right way. The patient had mild clouding of the eye lenses in both eyes. This started at a young age. The patient's hearing also got worse over time. A hearing test showed nerve-related hearing loss in both ears. A gene test found a change in a gene called GATA3. This change had not been seen before.

Affected Organ Systems:
The change in the GATA3 gene likely affects how certain organs grow before birth. These organs include the parathyroid gland, inner ear, and kidney.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should keep taking calcium lactate and 1α-hydroxyvitamin D3 as prescribed. The patient should get proper care for the mild eye lens clouding, hearing loss, and kidney problem. The patient should see doctors regularly to check for any changes in health.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]
Admission Diagnosis: Anthrax sore on the left upper eyelid
Discharge Diagnosis: The anthrax sore on the left upper eyelid is healing

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the clinic with a sore on the left upper eyelid. The sore was round, about half an inch wide, dark in color, and had a scab. It started 5 days before the visit. A sample was taken from the sore and tested. The test showed bacteria that matched anthrax germs. The patient had touched meat from a butcher shop in 2018 when anthrax was spreading in the area. The patient did not touch any sick animals directly. The patient was given two medicines to take by mouth. The first was ciprofloxacin 500 mg taken every 8 hours. The second was amoxicillin 875 mg plus clavulanic acid 125 mg taken every 12 hours. The patient also used chloramphenicol ointment on the sore twice a day. One day after starting treatment, the eyelid swelling got a little worse. A second sample was taken from the sore on day two. No bacteria grew because the medicines were already working.

By day seven, the sore was much better. The middle of the scab and the skin around it showed signs of healing. The eyelid swelling and redness went down. The patient stopped taking the medicines on day 16 because the sore had improved a lot. All body signs like heart rate and temperature stayed normal during the hospital stay.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was sent home with the following instructions. The patient should see their regular doctor for a follow-up visit. The patient should keep putting chloramphenicol ointment on the healing sore twice a day as told. The patient should wash hands well and often. The patient should stay away from animals and products that might carry germs. If the patient has new symptoms or worries, the patient should call their doctor.

The patient was admitted because of a low platelet count and mild bleeding symptoms. Platelets are blood cells that help stop bleeding. Many lab tests were done. The patient was found to have a rare genetic blood disorder called MYH9-related disease after genetic testing found a known gene change.

The patient had mild hearing loss and had nosebleeds and heavy periods since childhood. She had her spleen removed at age fifteen. She sometimes took a steroid medicine called prednisone when her platelet count dropped very low. The patient was correctly diagnosed with this blood disorder in 2016.

In 2018, she became pregnant and received very good care during pregnancy for herself and her babies. She received platelets one time at week 10 of pregnancy when her platelet count dropped a lot. At week 19 of pregnancy, scans of both twins showed a small fluid-filled sac in the brain of each baby. The babies' size, body parts, placenta position and shape, blood flow, and heart function were all normal. The twins were born at week 32 by surgery to deliver the babies. Both twins had low platelet counts, very large platelets, and medium-sized fluid-filled sacs in the brain at birth. Both babies were in good health, and one twin was smaller than most babies the same age. The mother received one dose of medicine to prevent bleeding before being put to sleep for surgery. Neither baby had any bleeding problems.

No medicines were prescribed when the patient left the hospital.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
A 9-year-old boy came to our hospital because he suddenly lost vision in his left eye 10 days earlier. This happened after he rubbed his eye very hard. When doctors checked his eyes, they found problems with both. The right eye had a bulging cornea (the clear front part of the eye) with stretch marks and a small surface scar. The left eye had severe swelling and a bulging cornea in the center. This showed a sudden fluid buildup. The doctors found that both eyes had a condition called keratoconus, where the cornea bulges outward. The left eye also had sudden swelling from fluid leaking into the cornea.

Treatment and Procedures:
The patient had a procedure on his left eye to fix the swelling. The doctor used a small needle to drain fluid from the front part of the eye in a clean, germ-free setting. Then the doctor filled this space with air. After that, the air was replaced with a special gas that filled two-thirds of the space. This gas helps push the cornea back into shape. The patient was given eye drops to prevent infection and reduce swelling. The patient was told to lie flat on his back after the procedure.

Outcome:
The patient has been checked by doctors for 12 months. The corneal swelling has completely gone away. The patient now has a light, cloudy scar on the cornea. With contact lenses, the patient can see 6/9, which is close to normal vision. The pressure inside the eye has stayed normal since the procedure.

Impressions and Plan:
The patient was treated for bulging corneas in both eyes and sudden swelling in the left eye. The special gas procedure was used to fix this. The corneal swelling has completely cleared up. The patient's vision has gotten better with contact lenses. The patient has been sent home and should keep seeing eye doctors for a long time.

The patient was a 54-year-old man who came to the hospital with ongoing fever and weight loss. Doctors ran many tests when the patient arrived. These included blood tests and tests to check how the liver and kidneys were working. Doctors also tested the blood for germs. All these tests came back normal.

Next, the patient had a special full-body scan called a PET-CECT. This scan showed unusual activity in the right side of the prostate gland. The prostate is a small gland below the bladder in men. None listed

Medical History:
The patient is a 50-year-old woman with HIV but is not taking HIV medicines.

Admission:
The patient came to the hospital with pain in the right side and lower belly for six months. The pain got worse over the past 15 days. The patient also had burning with urination and needed to urinate often, including at night, with sudden strong urges. There was no blood in the urine, no other bladder problems, and no fever. A physical exam showed tenderness in the lower belly and right side. The patient had low blood levels (7.6 g/dL) and received blood transfusions to fix this. Kidney function tests were normal.

Diagnosis:
An ultrasound of the kidneys, tubes, and bladder showed a small kidney stone (1.2 cm) in the right kidney and a bladder stone (1.7 cm). An X-ray did not show any stones. A CT scan of the same area showed only bladder stones.

Treatment:
Doctors looked inside the bladder and the tubes with small cameras and took tissue samples. The tissue samples showed the bladder lining had some sores and swelling with certain blood cells. There were no signs of cancer, abnormal cell growth, or other serious problems. Urine tests did not show any unusual protein crystals. Urine tests for infection were clear. Doctors removed the entire problem area through a procedure done through the urinary opening. The patient went home without any major problems after surgery.

Follow-Up:
The patient was asked to come back in six months for imaging tests and a camera exam of the bladder.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course:

A 42-year-old man with a history of diabetes and high blood pressure came to our hospital. He had repeated episodes of right arm and leg shaking, right face twitching, and trouble speaking clearly. These symptoms got worse with physical activity. At first, doctors thought he had a type of seizure and gave him seizure medicine called carbamazepine. The medicine did not stop his symptoms. More tests were done, including blood tests, heart rhythm tests, brain wave tests, and imaging scans. These tests showed a major blockage in the left neck artery that sends blood to the brain. Scans also showed a large buildup of plaque at the start of this artery. Doctors then believed his symptoms were caused by mini-strokes due to poor blood flow to the left side of his brain.

Treatment:

The patient received fluids through an IV and medicines to prevent blood clots, including clopidogrel and aspirin. He also received medicine to lower cholesterol called statins. Doctors did a procedure to open the blocked neck artery and placed a small tube called a stent to keep it open. Blood flow was restored very well after the procedure. The patient had no brain or nerve problems after the procedure. The procedure worked and completely stopped his symptoms. The patient continued taking blood clot prevention medicines and statins after the procedure. His arm and leg shaking and face twitching did not come back.

Clinical Courses:

The patient had no symptoms for at least 3 months and no new mini-strokes. He was sent home under the care of his regular doctor. He was told to keep taking his blood clot prevention medicines and statins. Doctors suggested follow-up visits to check on the artery blockage. The patient saw his regular doctor for follow-up, and no other problems were reported.

Diagnosis:

Mini-strokes with arm and leg shaking caused by a severe blockage in the left neck artery going to the brain.

Benefit and Risk:

The benefit of the procedure to open the artery and place the stent is that it restored blood flow to the left side of the brain. It also cleared up the symptoms. The patient continued taking blood clot prevention medicines and statins after the procedure. His arm and leg shaking and face twitching did not come back. The risks of this procedure may include the stent not working over time, stroke, infection, and bleeding. No problems happened in this case.

Follow-up:

The patient was told to see his regular doctor on a regular basis. These visits are to watch and manage his diabetes and high blood pressure. More follow-up visits were suggested to check on the artery blockage. The treatment plan may be changed if needed.

Prognosis:

The procedure to open the artery and place the stent worked well and stopped the patient's symptoms. The patient had no symptoms for at least 3 months and no new mini-strokes. How well the patient does in the future depends on taking medicines as directed and going to follow-up visits. It also depends on how well he manages his diabetes and high blood pressure.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 40-year-old woman who came to our clinic for left back pain that lasted 2 months. The physical exam showed nothing unusual. Blood tests showed slightly high levels of adrenaline and another hormone called renin. A detailed scan of the belly area showed growths on both adrenal glands, which are small organs above the kidneys. Doctors first thought these growths might be adrenal gland cancer. The patient had surgery to remove the left adrenal gland and the left kidney. Tests on the removed tissue showed unusual immune cells. More lab tests found that the patient had a rare type of cancer called NK/T-cell lymphoma, which is linked to a virus called EBV. The patient then had a full body scan to see where the cancer had spread. The scan showed the cancer was in the left adrenal gland area, the right adrenal gland, and under the skin of the left thigh.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was found to have NK/T-cell lymphoma linked to the EBV virus. The patient had surgery to remove the left adrenal gland and left kidney. After surgery, the patient received 7 rounds of cancer-fighting drugs using a treatment plan called GLIDE. The patient also had a transplant using their own stem cells. Two follow-up body scans done within one year showed the cancer was gone. There were no signs of cancer in any of the areas where it had been found before. The patient left the hospital with instructions to come back for check-up visits and ongoing care. This summary gives a full record of the patient's health history, treatment, and expected outcome.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient Name: [Confidential]

Admission Date: [Confidential]

Discharge Date: [Confidential]

Admission Diagnosis: Early stage breast cancer that had spread into nearby tissue. The cancer cells responded to some hormones but not others. The patient also had a gene change that raises breast cancer risk.

Hospital Course:

The patient was found to have early stage breast cancer. The cancer had started to spread into nearby breast tissue. Testing showed the cancer cells respond to some hormones. The patient also had a gene change called BRCA2 that raises cancer risk. She received drug treatment to shrink the cancer before surgery. Then she had surgery to remove both breasts. After surgery, she received more cancer drugs called trastuzumab and pertuzumab. The patient also started taking a hormone-blocking pill called toremifene.

Two years after finishing treatment, the patient found a swollen lymph node under her left arm. A tissue sample showed her breast cancer had come back. Three weeks later, the patient came to the emergency room. She had double vision, weight loss, and was urinating often. Scans showed the cancer had spread to her brain, liver, and neck bones.

The patient started radiation treatment aimed at the area around her eyes. She may also get radiation to a gland at the base of her brain. She restarted the cancer drugs trastuzumab and pertuzumab. She also began taking three new medicines called fulvestrant, goserelin, and zolendronic acid. The patient responded well to treatment. Her double vision got much better.

Discharge Diagnosis: Breast cancer that came back and spread to other parts of the body. The cancer cells respond to hormones.

Discharge Plan:

The patient will stay under close watch for her returning breast cancer that has spread. She will have more tests and scans as needed. Her cancer doctor will guide any new treatments. The patient will have regular check-up visits. Her care team will watch her health and change her treatment plan if needed.

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:

The patient is an 82-year-old Japanese male. He had small bumps and lumps on his belly, shoulders, arms, and legs for about 1 month. These bumps did not cause any pain or discomfort. The bumps on his forearms formed in clusters. The bumps on his belly appeared where he injects insulin for his type 2 diabetes. Blood tests showed signs of inflammation and high blood sugar levels over time. Calcium and ACE levels in the blood were normal.

The patient had an ultrasound test on the forearm bumps. The test showed areas around and inside blood vessels that may contain clumps of immune cells. A small piece of skin was taken from the belly bump for testing. The lab results showed clumps of immune cells without dead tissue in the deeper skin and fat layers.

The patient was diagnosed with sarcoidosis. This is a disease where clumps of immune cells form in different body parts. The disease affected his skin, muscles, and lymph nodes near both lungs. Doctors also found a single lump in a hip muscle using a special body scan. Eye and heart tests did not show any signs of the disease.

The patient was treated with a steroid cream. The belly skin bump almost went away. But the forearm bumps kept coming back along the veins over 1 year. The swollen lymph nodes near the lungs stayed the same size. One blood marker for inflammation did get better.

The patient should see specialists to keep checking on the sarcoidosis after leaving the hospital.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 75-year-old male patient came to the emergency room with a heart attack that happened some time before he arrived. He had high blood pressure, diabetes, and advanced Parkinson's disease treated with a brain device. A heart ultrasound showed that the lower left part of his heart was not pumping well and not moving. A test using dye showed that three blood vessels in his heart were blocked. The main problem was a fully blocked artery. Doctors used a small balloon and a tiny metal tube to open the blocked vessel. Blood flow was partly restored.

Hospitalization:
One day after the heart procedure, fluid suddenly built up in his lungs. His heartbeat became irregular. He needed medicine and a special pump placed in his main blood vessel to help his heart. A heart ultrasound showed a new problem. A heart valve was leaking badly. Part of the muscle holding the valve had torn. The pressure in the blood vessels going to his lungs was high at 55 mmHg.

Treatment:
The patient had other health problems. So the heart team chose to fix the leaky valve without open surgery. They used a clip system called MitraClip. The patient was moved to a procedure room. Doctors went through a vein and made a small hole between the upper heart chambers. They measured the pressure in the left upper chamber of the heart. The doctors put the patient to sleep. They used an ultrasound tube in his throat to guide them. They placed two small clips on the leaky valve. The clips were put in two spots to close the leak. The procedure worked well. The patient felt better right away.

Discharge:
The patient received good care during his hospital stay. He left the hospital one week after the clip procedure. A final heart ultrasound showed only a small amount of valve leak. The pressure was low. There were no major problems when he left. The care team told him to come back for follow-up visits.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
The patient is a 16-year-old boy who came to the eye emergency room. He had sudden vision loss in the lower half of his left eye.

Hospital Course:
During the eye exam, doctors found the patient could not see in the lower part of his vision. The blood vessels in the left eye also looked narrower than normal. The patient was told he had a blocked blood vessel in the upper part of his left eye. He was started on Aspirin. The patient was quickly sent to the stroke team for more tests.

The patient had an ultrasound of his heart, brain scans, and scans of blood vessels in the brain and neck. All of these tests came back normal. Blood tests showed high levels of a substance called homocysteine. The patient also had low vitamin B12 and slightly low folate levels. Later, a gene test found a change in a gene called MTHFR. This gene change can affect how the body uses certain vitamins.

Treatment:
The patient was given vitamin B12 and folate supplements. This brought the homocysteine levels back to normal. The patient also kept taking Aspirin.

Outcome:
A vision test two months later showed the patient's eyesight had gotten a little better. No new blood vessel blockages happened.

Summary:
The patient came in with sudden vision loss in the lower half of his left eye. This was caused by a blocked blood vessel in the upper part of the eye. Tests found a gene change called MTHFR that affects how the body processes vitamins. The patient was treated with vitamin B12 and folate supplements. The patient also continued taking Aspirin. A follow-up test at two months showed some improvement in vision.

Patient Identification:
Patient Name: Not Provided

Medical Record Number: Not Provided

Hospital Course:
The patient was brought to the hospital with several health problems. These included tiredness, weak muscles, skin problems, a swollen belly, peeing a lot, and drinking a lot of water. Blood tests and urine tests showed high blood sugar, high cholesterol, and sugar in the urine. After doctors confirmed the patient had diabetes, treatment began with a long-acting insulin called insulin glargine. The patient was also put on a special diet made for diabetic cats. The insulin dose was changed over time, and the patient got much better. A belly scan using sound waves showed that both adrenal glands were enlarged. The scan also showed fatty liver disease. More tests ruled out other conditions including growth hormone problems, overactive thyroid, and two cat viruses. However, doctors thought the patient might have a condition where the body makes too much of a stress hormone called cortisol. This condition is called Cushing's disease. It was confirmed using signs the patient showed, high cortisol levels in urine tests, and a special hormone test. A medicine called cabergoline was given to treat the Cushing's disease. After the second dose, the patient's blood sugar dropped too low. This needed emergency care from the vet. The low blood sugar was treated properly, and the patient was watched closely for several hours. After successful treatment and the health problems were under control, the patient went home.

Diagnosis:

Treatment:

The patient had steady blood sugar levels. There were no signs of diabetes or low blood sugar problems. Patient Identification:
The patient is a 69-year-old woman. She has serious glaucoma in her left eye. Glaucoma is a disease that damages the eye and can cause vision loss. Her glaucoma did not get better after surgery or eye drops.

Chief Complaint:
The patient came in because her left eye had an infection. The protective covering over part of her eye was also wearing away.

Hospital Course:
The patient had surgery to place a small drain in her left eye. This drain helps lower eye pressure. A patch was placed over the drain to protect it. After surgery, the patient used antibiotic eye drops four times a day for one week. She also used steroid eye drops to reduce swelling. She started at four times a day and slowly used less each week. The patient's skin problems healed with an antibiotic pill. Six weeks after the second surgery, there was no infection. The patch was still in good condition.

Impression:
The patient had surgery to place a drain for her glaucoma. There were problems after surgery that needed a second operation and antibiotics. The treatment was successful.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient will come back for regular checkups. Doctors will make sure the drain is working well.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Diagnosis: Fluid-filled sacs near the spine joints pressing on the bundle of nerves in the lower back

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted after several weeks of worsening back and left leg pain. The patient also had new problems urinating and leaking urine. The physical exam showed weakness in the left leg due to pain. The patient also had less feeling from the upper left thigh down to the top of the left foot and toes. An MRI scan of the lower back showed the spinal canal was very narrow at the L3-L4 level. This was caused by fluid-filled sacs near the spine joints on both sides, worse on the left. These sacs were pressing on the bundle of nerves in the lower back. A CT scan without dye also showed severe narrowing at L3-L4. X-rays taken while bending forward and backward showed the spine was stable.

After talking about treatment choices, the patient had surgery to remove the sacs. The surgeon also placed a Coflex device to keep the spine flexible and stable. This approach avoided using screws and rods while lowering the chance of the sacs coming back. Surgery happened three days after the first clinic visit. The surgeon removed parts of the L3 and L4 bones and joint edges through a cut in the middle of the back. The fluid-filled sacs were seen on both sides and fully removed using a surgical microscope. After relieving pressure on the nerves, a Coflex device was placed between the remaining L3 and L4 bones. The tissue was then closed in the normal way. The patient lost about 35cc of blood, which is a very small amount.

Lab tests confirmed the sacs were fluid-filled cysts from near the spine joints. After surgery, the patient had quick relief of left leg pain and no problems. The patient was moved to a rehab center one day after surgery. At the one-year checkup, the patient still has complete relief of left leg pain and urinary problems.

items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: Unknown
Gender: Female
Age: 61 years old
Admission Date: September 2012
Discharge Date: Unknown

Hospital Course:
The patient had worn-out knee joint cartilage in the right knee. She had surgery to replace the knee joint. During the hospital stay, her healing went smoothly. The patient left the hospital seven days after the surgery. However, at each check-up over nine months, she reported ongoing mild fever and swelling. She also had stiffness and pain in the knee that had surgery. These problems made it hard for her to do daily tasks. Doctors thought the area around the new knee joint might be infected. The patient was scheduled for surgery to clean the joint and replace parts of the knee. During the surgery, doctors did not find any clear signs of infection. They only found extra tissue growth and increased blood flow around the knee replacement. This was most noticeable in the area above the kneecap. Doctors found that the patient was allergic to the metal in the knee replacement. Only the plastic piece between the shin bone and metal parts was changed. The rest of the replacement was firmly in place. Treatment for the allergic reaction was started right after surgery. The patient felt much better after this treatment. Blood tests showed normal levels of most white blood cells. However, one type of white blood cell linked to allergies was higher than normal.

Follow-up:
Four years later, the patient's right knee was still slightly swollen. However, the pain was much better. The patient could fully straighten the knee and bend it to 90 degrees. All blood tests for swelling and irritation were normal. The allergy-related blood cells were also back to normal levels.

Impression:
The patient had worn-out cartilage in the right knee along with an allergy to metal. She had surgery to replace parts of the knee joint and received treatment for the allergic reaction. No signs of infection were found during the surgery. The patient felt much better afterward. Follow-up visits showed the knee moved better and blood tests returned to normal.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

HOSPITAL COURSE

The patient is a 49-year-old female who came in with red, swollen bumps on her private area for 2 months. She had been told at another hospital that she had a skin rash from touching something irritating. She took medicine for allergies, but it did not help. She also has had high blood pressure for 2 years and is allergic to a type of antibiotic called sulfonamide.

During her hospital stay, doctors found redness and swelling on her chest, belly, and private area. Her right leg was also swollen. There were flat bumps on the outer lips of her private area that were skin-colored or gray. Blood tests showed high levels of certain markers that can point to cancer.

The patient had several imaging tests done. These tests showed swelling and a small amount of fluid around the lungs. They also showed extra breast tissue growth and swollen lymph nodes throughout the body. There were also changes in and around the pancreas. Skin samples were taken and tested. The results showed a backup of a milky body fluid, which happens when there are too many white blood cells in one area.

A tissue sample was taken from the pancreas with a needle. It showed cancer that started in the pancreas. The cancer cells were growing at a medium to fast rate.

DISCUSSION

This patient had a rare case where cancer from the pancreas spread to other parts of the body. At first, doctors thought she had a skin rash from touching something irritating. But her symptoms did not go away, so doctors did more tests. They found cancer that had spread to many parts of her body, including her private area.

RECOMMENDATIONS

The patient was sent home with instructions to see doctors regularly at a medical center near her. She was told to think about cancer treatment choices with her cancer doctor. She was also told to watch her symptoms closely and follow her treatment plan.

Final Diagnosis: Inflammation of the heart muscle

Hospital Course:
A 7.5-year-old female came to the hospital with fever, crankiness, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhea, belly pain, red patchy rash all over the body, and had been around someone with COVID-19. When she arrived, the exam showed a red throat and red patchy rash all over the body. Blood tests showed low white blood cells and low vitamin D levels. The COVID-19 test came back negative. A chest scan, belly ultrasound, stool test, and cultures of urine, blood, and stool were all normal. The patient had been given diclofenac and azithromycin before coming to the hospital. She was then started on ceftriaxone, hydroxychloroquine, zinc, and vitamin D when she was admitted. On day three, swelling of the face, fast breathing, and fast heartbeat developed. The patient was found to have very low protein levels in the blood and low red blood cell count. She was given blood and protein through an IV. Waste products in the blood were high. A heart ultrasound showed the heart was not pumping well and both sides of the heart were enlarged. The patient was diagnosed with inflammation of the heart muscle. She was treated with medicines to support blood pressure, immune therapy given through an IV, and antibiotics called meropenem and vancomycin. She also got magnesium because her levels were low. A chest X-ray showed mild hazy spots in both lungs. On the fifth day, the patient still had fast heartbeat and fast breathing. Another dose of immune therapy was given along with aspirin. The blood pressure medicines were slowly reduced as the patient's heart function got better. On the seventh day, the patient no longer had a fever. She was sent home after 12 days with a normal heart ultrasound and normal lab tests.

Patient: 23-year-old female

Chief complaint: Swollen gums and loose teeth

Medical history: No past health problems.

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the Gum Disease Department at Seoul National University Dental Hospital in 2004. The patient had swollen gums. The patient was told earlier that she had a serious type of gum disease that spreads quickly. The patient had deep cleaning of teeth and roots along with pills to fight infection. The patient said she first noticed swollen gums and loose teeth when she was 13 years old. The patient had gum treatment and was sent to the Tooth Replacement Department for more care.

The goals of treatment were to teach the patient about oral care and get her involved in her treatment. Other goals were to help the patient clean her mouth better, improve how her teeth look, and get results that last. Several teeth were removed. These included the pointed tooth in the upper jaw and some front and side teeth in the lower jaw. At first, the plan was to place metal posts in the upper jaw bone to hold fixed fake teeth. But the jaw bone shrank very fast after the teeth were pulled. So the plan changed to fake teeth that snap onto metal posts but can be taken out. The dental team made molds and models of the mouth to plan the new teeth.

The team tested wax models of the upper teeth and a strong white frame for the lower teeth. Then the final new teeth were put in place. The patient was taught how to clean between teeth every day using special cleaning tools. A care plan was set up with gum checkups every 3 months after getting the final teeth.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was sent home with directions on how to keep her mouth clean. The patient will have gum checkups every 3 months after getting the final teeth.

Follow-up:

The patient will need to see her dentist for regular checkups to keep her mouth healthy.

The patient is a 75-year-old white female. She came to the emergency room feeling dizzy and weak. She also felt full quickly after eating and had chest heaviness. These symptoms got worse over time. The patient did not have belly pain, nausea, vomiting, blood in stool, dark tarry stool, or bone pain. In the past, she had heartburn and small pouches in her colon. She also used pain relievers like ibuprofen regularly.

During the exam, the patient looked pale and had a fast heartbeat. A stool test showed hidden blood. Blood tests showed low red blood cell levels at 7.6, which is below normal. Doctors looked for the source of bleeding in the stomach and intestines. A camera test looking at the food pipe, stomach, and upper intestine showed irritation and sores in the stomach and upper intestine. It also showed a thin ring of tissue where the food pipe meets the stomach. This ring was not blocking anything. Tissue samples from the stomach and intestine showed a type of cancer cell. Doctors first thought this cancer started in the stomach. However, more tests found a type of breast cancer that had spread to the chest wall and the lining of the belly.

The patient received one bag of donated blood and felt better. She then started a hormone-blocking medicine called anastrozole. Later, she started another cancer medicine called palbociclib.

Doctors thought the cancer most likely started in the breast. They took a deep tissue sample from lumps under the breast. They also did a surgery using a small camera to look inside the belly. During this surgery, they took tissue samples from the area near the liver and lower belly lining. The patient felt very upset and worried after learning about the cancer. She received support and counseling from trained staff.

Doctors found that the breast cancer had spread to the bone marrow. The patient has an appointment set up with her cancer doctor.

The patient has an appointment set up with her cancer doctor. She should also see her regular doctor as soon as possible. This is to help manage her health conditions. The patient should get all the tests and scans her doctors recommend.

The patient is taking a hormone-blocking medicine called anastrozole. She will also take a cancer medicine called palbociclib. The patient should keep taking all her medicines as her doctors tell her.

The patient came in with pain when swallowing and trouble swallowing food. The patient was found to have late-stage throat cancer. The patient had surgery to remove the voice box and part of the throat. The patient also had lymph nodes removed from the left side of the neck. After surgery, the patient received cancer-killing drugs and radiation at the same time. Scans taken before and during treatment showed no problems at the base of the skull. But four months after treatment ended, the patient started seeing double and had a drooping eyelid. A brain scan showed a growth near a small gland at the base of the brain. The patient had surgery through the nose to remove this growth. After that, the patient received six rounds of cancer-killing drugs and radiation to the base of the skull. The treatment did not work well, and the original cancer kept growing. The patient lost the ability to move both vocal cords and had heavy nosebleeds from time to time. A spine scan showed the cancer had spread to several bones in the spine. Some bones in the upper back broke and pressed on the spinal cord. The patient's health kept getting worse until the patient died because many organs stopped working.

Discharge Diagnosis:
A fast-growing cancer that spread, with some cells showing nerve-like features

Discharge Instructions:
The patient has been sent home from the hospital with instructions for end-of-life care. The patient's family has been told about the patient's condition. Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male
Age: 36 years
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with fever and trouble breathing for 15 days. He also had a dry cough and dark, bloody stool for five days. Tests for liver diseases and other causes did not give clear answers. The patient had swollen veins in his food pipe. His past health history included liver damage from alcohol use. This was his second hospital stay in two months. During his first stay, he had low levels of two types of blood cells. This was likely caused by his liver disease. He had fluid buildup around his right lung during both hospital stays. This fluid was caused by pressure, not infection. On this visit, tests of the lung fluid showed a bacterial infection called E. coli on the third day. Doctors gave him antibiotics called Piperacillin/Tazobactam 4.5 grams every 6 hours when he arrived. They later changed this to ceftriaxone based on his medical records. His breathing problems were later treated with another antibiotic called levofloxacin.

Follow-up:
The patient later had a bacterial infection in his belly fluid and lung fluid during his next hospital stay. These were treated with antibiotics and medicine to help his liver work better. Five months later, the patient came back with fluid around his lung and fever. He was treated with an antibiotic called amikacin for ten days. Seven months after that, the patient returned with belly and lung fluid infections. He also had very bad trouble breathing and a large amount of fluid around his lungs. Doctors drained fluid from his belly and lungs several times. His breathing did not get better. He then had bleeding in his stomach and went into shock. Sadly, these problems led to his death.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Liver damage from alcohol use with repeated bacterial infections in the lung fluid and belly fluid.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient's family was told to get medical help right away if the patient shows signs of breathing problems or liver problems.

Follow-up:
The patient's family was told to make a follow-up visit with the patient's regular doctor within one month after leaving the hospital.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]   Date of Admission: [REDACTED]    Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes that was not well controlled and a very enlarged liver.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 11-year old boy with type 1 diabetes, was brought to the Emergency Room. He was urinating a lot, very thirsty, losing weight, and feeling weak. He had a serious problem called diabetic ketoacidosis, where the body has too much acid in the blood. He was given insulin through an IV following standard guidelines for children. After a week, he was sent home with a plan to take insulin shots every day. The patient did not come back for his scheduled visit at the Diabetes Centre. Because of this, his blood sugar stayed poorly controlled and he had more episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis.

At age 10, the patient moved to Southern Italy with his family. He was then brought to our Children's Diabetes Clinic after another serious episode of diabetic ketoacidosis. At that time, he also had a very enlarged liver and was shorter than expected for his age. He had not started puberty yet, and his hormone levels were checked.

Blood tests were done to find the cause of his enlarged liver. Tests ruled out liver disease caused by the immune system and infections. A small sample of liver tissue showed no swelling or scarring. The doctors confirmed that his liver was storing too much sugar, a condition called hepatic glycogenosis.

While in the hospital, the patient learned how to manage his diabetes. His daily insulin dose was adjusted to help control his blood sugar. A check-up three months later showed his blood sugar was still poorly controlled. He also had a very enlarged liver and unhealthy fat levels in his blood. He was admitted to the hospital again.

During this second hospital stay, the patient received insulin through an IV to bring his liver enzyme levels back to normal. The goal was also to get his blood sugar under control. This was reached after eight days. At his last check-up, the patient's blood sugar was well controlled. His lab results and symptoms had improved, and his liver was back to normal size.

Diagnostic Impression:
The patient has type 1 diabetes that was not well controlled, a very enlarged liver, and a condition where the liver stores too much sugar.

Follow-Up Recommendations:
The patient should keep following his diabetes care plan and see his doctor regularly. The patient should also have his blood fat levels checked from time to time.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [redacted] Ethnicity: Unknown Age: 81 Gender: Male
Date of admission: [redacted] Date of discharge: [redacted]
Length of stay: 40 days
Admitting Diagnosis: Infected pouches in the lower bowel, infected appendix, and a pocket of infection that spread behind the belly organs

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital after 4 days of not wanting to eat and belly pain. The patient then fell and lay on the floor for 14 hours. This led to a pocket of infection on the left side of the body. The exam showed signs of belly lining swelling, fast heartbeat, low blood pressure, and fast breathing. These signs pointed to a serious body-wide infection. The patient also had long-term kidney problems and was overweight. A special scan of the belly and pelvis showed infected pouches in the lower bowel. This infection caused a pocket of pus that spread behind the belly organs. The patient also had an infected appendix.

Surgery was needed because the patient was very sick. The patient also had other health problems that made surgery risky. These included heart disease from poor blood flow, an uneven heartbeat, and late-stage kidney disease caused by cysts on the kidneys. The doctors removed part of the lower bowel, closed off the remaining part, and made a new opening in the belly for waste to leave the body. This is called Hartmann's procedure. The doctors also removed the appendix. A small amount of infection fluid was found on the left side of the belly. The area behind the belly organs was not opened during surgery. Tubes were placed to drain fluid from the left side of the belly and the pelvis.

After surgery, the patient was taken off the breathing machine on day 1. The patient stayed in the intensive care unit for 8 days. This was because the patient needed extra oxygen due to a lung infection. The patient then moved to the regular surgery ward. The patient later got a worse body-wide infection. Another scan showed a large pocket of infected fluid behind the belly organs on the left side. Two drain tubes were placed through the skin into this pocket of fluid. Even with infection-fighting medicine given through a vein and draining the fluid, the patient died on day 40 after surgery. The cause of death was the worsening body-wide infection.

Summary of Hospital Course:
The 81-year-old male patient came in with infected pouches in the lower bowel, an infected appendix, and a pocket of infection that spread behind the belly organs. These problems led to surgery. During the hospital stay, the patient got a lung infection that needed care in the intensive care unit. Later, the patient got a worse body-wide infection. The patient died on day 40 after surgery.

Discharge Diagnoses:
1. Infected pouches in the lower bowel
2. Infected appendix
3. Pocket of infection that spread behind the belly organs

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was released to the care of his regular doctor. The patient's family was told to watch for any changes in his health. This includes fever, pain, or discomfort. They should get medical help if these changes happen. They were also told to share his medical history, surgery details, and this hospital stay with any doctor who treats him soon after leaving the hospital. No other instructions are needed after leaving the hospital.

Patient Discharge Summary

Patient Name: Not disclosed
Date of admission: Not disclosed
Date of discharge: Not disclosed

Admission Diagnoses: High blood pressure, High cholesterol, Diabetes, Heart attack (a type that does not show major changes on heart rhythm tests)

Medical History: The patient had a history of high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted to the heart care unit because of sudden chest pain while resting. Heart rhythm tests and blood tests showed signs of a heart attack. An ultrasound of the heart showed the heart wall was thicker than normal. It also showed part of the lower heart wall was not moving as well as it should. The heart was still pumping normally overall. The ultrasound found an unusual blood flow pattern inside the lower heart wall. This blood flow was moving from the heart wall into the main pumping chamber. The flow path ran under one of the heart valves.

Treatment: Based on medical guidelines, the patient had a high risk score for heart problems. Doctors recommended a procedure to open blocked heart arteries within 24 hours. The patient had a test where dye was put into the heart arteries to look for blockages. This test showed several arteries were narrowed or blocked. The main artery on the front of the heart was 90 percent blocked in one spot and 70 percent blocked in another. Other arteries had 50 to 70 percent blockages. The test also showed an unusual extra blood vessel. This vessel connected a heart artery to the inside of the heart pumping chamber. The patient had a procedure to open the blocked arteries. Doctors placed two small mesh tubes in the front artery and one mesh tube in another artery. These tubes are coated with medicine to keep the arteries open.

Follow up: The patient had a heart scan to get a better picture of the unusual extra blood vessel. The scan showed where this vessel started, where it traveled, and where it drained into the heart chamber. At a checkup 24 months later, the patient had no symptoms.

Disposition: The patient was sent home in good condition.

That surgery removed part of the bone in the lower spine at the L4-5 level. The physical exam and brain and nerve tests were normal. The doctors found that the headache was caused by spinal fluid leaking. The patient was told to stay in bed. A treatment was done where the patient's own blood was put into the spine to seal the leak. This did not help. A brain scan was normal. Then a different type of blood patch was done on the left side at the L3-4 and L4-5 levels. After this treatment, the headache and other symptoms went away without any problems.

At the 2-week checkup, the patient had no headache. The patient was back to normal activities.

The patient was told to rest in bed, drink plenty of fluids, and take acetaminophen for pain. Blood patch treatments were done to seal the leak. The first was done at the L2-3 level using 15ml of the patient's own blood. This was repeated at the L4-5 level with the same amount of blood. Finally, a different type of blood patch was done at L3-4 and L4-5 on the left side using 3ml of blood at each level.

Follow-up Care:
