Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: 1995
Discharge Date: Not available

Chief Complaint:
Feeling unwell, nose bleeds, and sinus infection.

History of Present Illness:
A 26-year-old male came in feeling unwell with nose bleeds and a sinus infection in 1995. A blood test showed signs of a disease that attacks blood vessels. A tissue sample from the nose matched a condition called Wegener's disease. No other body parts were affected at that time. Treatment started with a strong medicine through a vein, a steroid pill, and an antibiotic. The disease stayed active despite treatment. The patient later developed narrowing in the airway below the voice box and in the right lung tube.

Past Medical History:
Not listed in the case report.

Medications:
Not listed in the case report.

Allergies:
Not listed in the case report.

Social History:
Not listed in the case report.

Family History:
Not listed in the case report.

Physical Examination:
Not listed in the case report.

Diagnostic Testing:
Blood tests showed swelling markers were high at a regular checkup in 2004. A brain scan showed the pituitary gland was swollen with a thickened stalk. This pointed to swelling of the pituitary gland but no tumor. Scans of the sinus behind the nose showed heavy swelling and a hole in the wall between the nostrils.

Hospital Course:
The patient had active sinus and airway disease that caused the nose bridge to collapse. The patient received a special immune system medicine between 1996 and 2002. The patient also took a short round of a strong pill medicine in 1999. The narrowed airway needed steroid shots and stretching. A low dose of steroid pills helped manage this problem.

At regular checkups, the patient reported passing too much urine and feeling very thirsty. This was very hard to live with. A brain scan showed the sinus swelling was getting worse and the pituitary gland was getting bigger. The patient was told the Wegener's disease had caused a problem making the body lose too much water. A nose spray medicine was started to control this water loss problem. The symptoms got better with this medicine. In December 2005, the patient received strong medicines through a vein to control the disease. Two rounds of another immune system medicine followed to stop the disease from getting worse.

Summary:
In summary, a 26-year-old male came in feeling unwell with nose bleeds and a sinus infection. These problems matched Wegener's disease. The patient developed narrowing in the airway and lung tube. Treatment included strong medicines through a vein, steroid pills, and an antibiotic. The disease stayed active despite treatment. The patient then received special immune system medicines and a short course of strong pills. The pituitary gland became swollen, which led to a water loss problem. The patient used a nose spray medicine to control this. Strong medicines through a vein and immune system medicines helped control the disease from getting worse.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Female
Age: 18 years
Admit Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the bone and joint unit for a broken upper arm bone that was not healing. The break was in the lower part of the left upper arm bone. The patient had no other health problems and did not report any injury. At first, doctors used a partial plaster cast, then a full plaster cast. However, imaging showed the bone was not growing back together. Over time, imaging showed the bone was slow to heal, breaking down, and becoming weak and thin. Doctors thought the patient had a bone infection and treated it, but she did not get better. She was then sent to our hospital for more care.

During the stay, doctors checked the patient's left arm closely. They found weak muscles throughout the arm and limited movement in the forearm. Moving the shoulder and elbow caused mild pain and was limited. The wrist moved normally, gripping was fine, and there were no nerve problems. Imaging showed much of the bone had disappeared at the break site. This left a gap of about one inch with pointed bone ends and thin, weak bone overall. More tests including blood work, bone scans, and detailed imaging ruled out other causes of bone loss and cancer. A sample of bone tissue confirmed the patient has Gorham-Stout Syndrome in the left upper arm bone. This is a rare disease where bone disappears and is replaced by blood vessel growth.

Treatment:

The patient had surgery to rebuild the left upper arm bone using bone taken from the lower leg bone. This matches what medical research says works well for this rare disease in the arm.

Follow-up:

The patient left the hospital in stable condition with instructions for care after surgery. She should see the bone and joint surgeon regularly to check how the bone is healing. No new problems were reported.

Diagnosis: Gorham-Stout Syndrome of the left upper arm bone. This is a rare disease that causes bone to slowly disappear.

To check if the heart muscle was inflamed, doctors did a special scan of the heart using magnets. This scan showed a small area of heart muscle damage on the back wall of the lower left heart chamber.

Doctors then used a special camera inside the blood vessel to get a closer look. This confirmed there was a blood clot that was not fully blocking the artery.

The patient got better over time. The symptoms did not come back and the heart stress markers in the blood went down. Later heart tracing tests showed some changes in the wave patterns.

Medications on Discharge: Blood thinner medicine, cholesterol-lowering medicine

The patient should keep taking all medicines as directed. The patient must not eat any fish. The patient should see a heart doctor in three months for a heart ultrasound and heart tracing test to check healing. If symptoms come back, the patient should get medical help right away.

Re-narrowing of the main blood vessel and a bulge in the vessel wall that could burst.

Blood vessel repair using mesh tubes placed inside the vessel and widening of a narrow section using a special balloon.

After that, the patient took antibiotic pills called co-trimoxazole three times a day for 12 weeks. The fever and joint pain went away. A follow-up ultrasound showed the infected fluid pocket had healed. The chest X-ray showed the lung problem was getting better.

The patient was told to keep taking medicines for health problems that existed before this illness. The patient and family were taught how to check blood sugar levels. They also received advice about healthy eating and exercise.

The patient learned why it is important to take all medicines and follow healthy habits to control this disease. The patient was told to get medical help right away if symptoms get worse. None specified.

The patient died on day 3 in the nursing home. The cause of death is not known. The family chose not to have an exam of the body after death.

The patient was admitted to the hospital because of a leak around her artificial heart valve. She had surgery to fix this leak. The patient had heart valve surgery three times before. The first was 47 years ago to open a stiff valve. The second was in 1975 to put in an artificial valve. The third was in 2005 to replace the valve because scar tissue had grown on it. Also, one year ago, the patient had a procedure at another hospital to treat an irregular heartbeat. Doctors used heat energy to block the faulty electrical signals in her heart. The treatment worked at first, but her heart got weaker over the following months.

The patient had severe heart failure that limited all physical activity. An ultrasound of her heart through the chest wall showed a medium-sized leak around the valve. Her heart was pumping at a normal strength of 60 percent. Another ultrasound done through the throat showed a medium to large leak on the back outer side of the valve. The patient chose surgery instead of a less invasive option to fix the leak. Before the heat treatment one year ago, regular heart ultrasounds showed no leak or high pressure in the lung blood vessels. The leak appeared three months after the heat treatment.

After surgery, the patient was taken off the breathing machine within 12 hours. The medicine helping her heart pump was also stopped. None

Identification: 26-year-old female found to have asthma at the age of 16

Admission Date: October 2018

Discharge Date: July 2019

Main Problem: Asthma and growths in the nose called polyps

Hospital Stay:

The patient came in with a history of nose polyps. These had been removed by surgery eight years before but came back in the past two years.
The patient was treated with steroid medicine breathed into the lungs. The patient reported losing the sense of smell. Tests for common things that cause allergies were negative.
The patient had sour breath with blocked airways throughout the lungs.
Blood tests showed high levels of a white blood cell type called eosinophils at 1200 per unit. A marker for allergies called IgE was 126 units. A breathing test showed the lungs were working at 70 percent. A score for asthma control was 14.
Treatment included inhaled steroids with a long-acting inhaler to open airways. A second type of long-acting inhaler was added a few months before. The patient also took steroid pills called prednisone at 25 mg daily for the past 3 months.
In October 2018, a new medicine called benralizumab was started.
On day 28, no eosinophils were found in the blood. The allergy marker dropped to 38 units. Lung function and symptom control both got better.
The amount of steroid pills had been lowered.
At the last visit in July 2019, eosinophils were still not found in the blood. The allergy marker was down to 26 units. The patient continued to improve in symptoms and lung function.
Steroid pills had been stopped three months before this visit.
The patient had no asthma flare-ups, hospital stays, or emergency room visits while on benralizumab.

Discharge Diagnosis: Asthma with nose polyps

Condition at Discharge: Stable

Plan: The patient should follow up with their regular doctor. No other specific treatments are needed.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: N/A
Gender: Male
Age: 53 years
Hospital Admission Date: N/A
Date of Discharge: N/A

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for an eye infection called toxoplasmosis in his left eye. This infection caused swelling in the back of the eye. The patient had this eye infection before and had antibodies showing past exposure to the parasite. The patient was treated with several medicines before, and the infection in the back of the eye got better. However, swelling and floating cells in the front of the eye continued. New problems appeared, including round areas of tissue damage around the entire colored part of the eye. The colored part of the eye also stuck to the lens, and eye pressure became too high. Doctors thought a virus might be causing some of these problems. The patient was started on antiviral medicine and medicines to reduce swelling. Later, the patient developed clouding in the lens of the left eye and needed surgery. The patient also had the eye swelling come back in the left eye, even with treatment.

FINDINGS:
More eye exams showed twisted blood vessels on the white part of the eye. There were some floating cells in the front of the eye. The round areas of tissue damage around the colored part of the eye had spread. Some areas showed deeper damage where inner tissue fibers could be seen. There was also a small spot where light passed through abnormally. The pupil was uneven in shape and partly widened. The patient had an artificial lens from past surgery. Looking at the back of the left eye showed the gel inside was breaking down. The gel had also pulled away from the back of the eye. There were some floating cells in the gel. The nerve at the back of the eye had a small cup shape. There was also a light-colored scar on the lower outer part of the back of the eye.

LABORATORY FINDINGS:
Lab tests and fluid samples from the eye were taken. The tests found genetic material from the chickenpox virus and the toxoplasmosis parasite. The tests ruled out several other viruses, including herpes type 1 and type 2, and other related viruses. The patient tested positive for antibodies to the chickenpox virus.

TREATMENT:
The patient was treated with medicines to fight the parasite, antiviral medicine, and medicines to reduce swelling. Eye drops to widen the pupil were given until the swelling in the front of the eye went away.

FOLLOW-UP:
After four weeks of treatment, the patient said he felt better. Doctors observed that the swelling inside the eye had gone away.

IMPRESSION:
The patient was found to have an eye infection from a parasite and had antibodies showing past exposure. The patient later had the eye swelling come back in his left eye. More tests found genetic material from both the chickenpox virus and the parasite. The patient received treatment and got better after four weeks.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
No discharge instructions are given as the patient has not been discharged.

The patient, a 6-year-old Greek boy, came to our hospital with a painful swelling in the left groin area. Before coming here, the patient went to another hospital. The sac stretched about 7 cm long. It contained a small piece of fatty tissue from inside the belly. Doctors pushed this tissue back into place. They closed the weak spot using stitches that do not dissolve over time.

The patient stayed in good condition during the hospital stay. The patient went home without any problems. The patient was told to rest. The patient was given instructions for follow-up care.

Follow-Up Care:

The patient has had no symptoms and the hernia has not come back for eight years after the surgery.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: IA, Mr.
Age: 85
Sex: Male

Hospital Course:
Mr. IA, an 85-year-old male, came to the mental health clinic. He was seeing things that were not there. He saw images of people in front of him. He had been treated for high pressure in his eyes for 7 years. This condition affects both eyes and can damage vision. He had been unable to see for the past 3 years. These strange visions had been happening for about 8 weeks before his visit. The doctor checked his eyes and found damage to the back of both eyes. The light-sensitive area in each eye had dried out and broken down. The nerve that connects the eye to the brain looked pale and showed signs of damage in both eyes. All other body and brain tests were normal for his age.

Treatment and Response:
The patient was told that he did not have a mental illness. He learned a way to make the images go away. He was told to close his eyes and blink over and over. This could make the images disappear for a short time before coming back. His family members learned about this condition called Charles Bonnet Syndrome. They were told not to think of it as a mental illness. At first, the patient came back every 2 weeks. Later, visits were spread out to every 4 weeks and then every 6 weeks. His eyesight did not get better during this time. However, the visions went away after 6 months without any medicine. He was then sent home from care.

Condition at Discharge:
Mr. IA left with a clear understanding of the eye-closing and blinking method used to help him. He was reminded not to think of this as a mental illness. He was told to close his eyes often and blink many times if the visions came back. His family members were happy with the information and advice they received. They agreed to watch and make sure the method was being used and working.

Hospital Course Summary:

This is a hospital course summary for a 15-year-old girl who came to the hospital because she had very little urine output and blood in her urine for 20 days after having a cold. She was found to have a type of kidney disease where the body's immune system attacks the small blood vessels in the kidneys. The cause of her high platelet count was not known.

Treatment:
During her hospital stay, the patient had a treatment to clean her blood 3 times a week. She also received high doses of two medicines through an IV to calm her immune system. These medicines were Methylprednisolone and Cyclophosphamide. She also had a treatment to filter and replace part of her blood. Other treatments helped control her blood pressure and protect her stomach lining.

Outcome:
When the patient left the hospital, her kidney waste levels had dropped to 313.8 units per liter. Her platelet count was 439 billion per liter. The patient kept getting high-dose Cyclophosphamide treatments at regular times for 3 more rounds. Up until now, her platelet count has stayed below 500 billion per liter.

Diagnosis:
The final diagnosis was RT.

Follow-up:
The patient was checked on for 6 months after leaving the hospital. Her platelet count stayed within the normal range during this time.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Stay:

The patient came to the hospital after being stabbed in the left side of the chest. When he arrived at the emergency room, his blood pressure was very low. His heart was beating too fast, and he was breathing too fast. He was also slightly less alert than normal. A quick scan showed fluid had collected around his left lung. Doctors put in a tube to drain the fluid, and more than 700 mL of blood came out. Another scan showed fluid had also collected around his heart.

Doctors had to open the patient's chest because his condition was not stable. During surgery, they found a large amount of blood in the left chest area. They also found damage to the back part of the left lung and the sac around the heart. Blood and clots had built up around the heart. There was a small hole in the right side of the heart near a major blood vessel. Doctors used medicine to temporarily stop the heart so they could fix the hole with stitches. The patient recovered after surgery and stayed in the intensive care unit for 13 days.

Discharge Summary:

The patient left the hospital after 13 days with no problems. Heart scans after surgery showed some damage to the wall between the heart chambers. However, the patient did not show any signs that the heart was not pumping well.

The patient should not do hard physical activities and should rest for at least two weeks. It is important to watch for signs of infection, such as fever, redness or swelling, and fluid leaking from the wound. The patient should tell a doctor right away about any chest pain, trouble breathing, or feeling dizzy.

The patient should see a regular doctor or heart doctor within one week, depending on how he is doing. He should go back to the hospital right away if new problems start or current problems get worse.

The patient is doing well right now and has gone home with the care plan described above.

Discharge Summary:

Patient:
A 5-month-old baby girl with a hernia in the left groin area that she was born with. The hernia contained her uterus and fallopian tubes.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital because of swelling in her left groin area. The swelling showed up when she cried and had been there since birth. The doctor examined her and found swelling in the left groin that went down to the outer part of her private area. The swelling could be pushed back in. The doctor determined she had a hernia she was born with. Surgery was planned to fix the hernia. During surgery, the doctors found a large hernia sac with a firm mass inside. The doctors cut open the sac and tied it off. They gently pushed the uterus and connected tubes back into the belly where they belong.

Finding:
The uterus and fallopian tubes were found inside the hernia sac. The opening to the hernia was wide enough to fit the tip of a small finger.

Diagnosis:
A hernia in the left groin area that the patient was born with. The hernia contained the uterus and fallopian tubes.

Plan:
The patient had surgery to fix the hernia. The uterus and fallopian tubes were freed from the hernia sac. They were pushed back into the belly. The opening was stitched closed to make it smaller. No more treatment is needed. The patient should heal completely.

Follow-up:
The patient should be watched for any signs the hernia comes back or other problems. A follow-up visit with the doctor should be scheduled as directed.

items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Not provided
Date of Admission: Not provided
Date of Discharge: Not provided

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission: The patient came to the hospital with two weeks of pain in the side of the back and four days of dark brown urine. During the physical exam, the heart had a normal beat with an extra heart sound heard best on the left side of the chest. The patient had strong pain when the doctor pressed on the left side of the back near the kidney. The doctor also heard crackling sounds in the lower parts of both lungs. First blood tests showed low white blood cell count, low red blood cell count, and low platelet count. The tests also showed high creatinine levels, which means the kidneys were not working well. The urine test was not normal.

Diagnosis: The patient was found to have a blocked blood vessel in the spleen, which damaged part of the spleen. The patient also had a heart valve that formed with two flaps instead of three. This valve had a growth on it caused by an infection. The infection did not show up in blood tests that look for germs. A small tissue sample was taken from the kidney. It showed the immune system was causing swelling and damage in the kidney.

Treatment: The patient took two antibiotics called doxycycline and rifampin for 6 weeks. The patient also had surgery to replace the damaged heart valve. During treatment, the side pain got better. There were fewer red blood cells in the urine. The creatinine levels went down, which means the kidneys were working better.

Prognosis: The patient got better during treatment. However, a blood test for a certain protein linked to the immune system stayed high even after taking antibiotics.

Follow-up: The patient should see a regular doctor for checkups. More tests may be needed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: [Name]
Date of Admission: [Admission Date]
Date of Discharge: [Discharge Date]
Admitting Diagnosis: Sudden kidney problems, leg swelling, trouble breathing at rest, no fever, yellow skin, and open sores with dead tissue

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 58-year-old male, came to the hospital because he was not making much urine, had swollen legs, and had trouble breathing while resting. The exam showed the patient had no fever but had yellow skin and open sores with dead tissue on the inner thighs. Blood tests showed the kidneys were not working well. Liver tests were also higher than normal. The patient's blood showed signs that the immune system was not working right. Some antibody tests came back high, while others were normal.

An ultrasound of the belly showed the kidneys looked normal in size with no calcium deposits. The liver ultrasound showed two dark spots in both sides of the liver with no blood flow.

Doctors thought a blood cancer with abnormal proteins might be causing the nerve problems and blood vessel damage in the skin. The patient's kidney function and skin sores got better with water pills and high-dose steroids.

A sample of liver tissue taken on day three showed a type of cancer called MALT lymphoma that started in the liver. There were no signs of this cancer in other parts of the body.

The patient was sent to a cancer doctor and started a treatment plan called R-CHOP. Three months after leaving the hospital, the patient came back with severe liver failure that led to death. Tests showed high levels of hepatitis B and hepatitis D viruses even though earlier blood tests did not show signs of infection.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient should get medical help right away if there is new or worse yellow skin, fever, belly pain, or other worrying signs. The patient should not drink alcohol, take products with acetaminophen, or take any medicines without asking a doctor first. The patient's medical records and tissue test results should be shared with any future doctors or nurses.

Patient Information:
Name: Confidential
Age: 67 years old
Sex: Male
Date of admission: April 13, 2011
Date of discharge: April 27, 2011

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital for a heart artery test. An earlier scan showed a possible problem with the heart arteries. The test found one heart artery was 80 percent blocked. Doctors placed a small mesh tube coated with medicine to open the blocked artery. Soon after, the patient's heart stopped beating. This happened because the artery got a hole near the mesh tube. Doctors put a breathing tube through the nose and drained fluid from around the heart. This helped the blood flow normally again. Tiny metal coils were placed to close the hole. The hole sealed and no more blood leaked around the heart.

More pictures of the heart showed blood clots. One clot was in the main heart artery. Another clot was inside the new mesh tube. Doctors used a device to suction out the clots. The patient also received blood-thinning medicine through a vein. The patient stayed stable and moved to the heart care unit. The patient left the hospital two weeks later with no chest pain during activity and normal heart function.

The patient received blood-thinning shots under the skin for 7 days. There were no problems during this time. The patient was checked for more than one year after leaving the hospital. No problems were reported.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 50 years
Sex: Female
Race: South Indian

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the clinic with a cough that brought up mucus and blood for the past 2 months. She had lung tuberculosis before but stopped taking her medicine within 3 weeks of starting it. She also has diabetes with nerve damage in her hands and feet for the past 8 years. She takes pills to control her blood sugar. The patient was found to have a fungus ball growing in her lung. She was treated with an antifungal medicine called Voriconazole, first at a higher dose, then at a lower dose. The patient got better with treatment. The coughing up of blood stopped after surgery to remove part of her lung. After 3 weeks, tests showed no more tuberculosis germs in her mucus. The patient is now in month 4 of treatment and is doing well.

Laboratory Results:
Tests done when the patient arrived showed low red blood cells. Her kidney and liver were working normally.

Diagnostic Study:
A CT scan of the chest showed a hollow space with thick walls in the upper part of the right lung. A fungus ball was growing inside this space. Three mucus samples tested positive for tuberculosis germs using a special staining test. Lab growth tests confirmed the germ was tuberculosis. Drug testing showed the tuberculosis was resistant to two main medicines, Isoniazid and Rifampicin. The tuberculosis could still be treated with Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and Streptomycin.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with lung tuberculosis and a fungus ball in the lung.

Treatment:
The patient first started taking daily doses of Isoniazid, Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide, and Streptomycin. After tests showed drug-resistant tuberculosis, Isoniazid was stopped. Two new medicines, Levofloxacin and Ethionamide, were added. Rifampicin was not used because it does not work well with the antifungal medicine. For the fungus ball, the patient took Voriconazole 400 mg twice for the first day. Then she took 200 mg twice a day for 6 weeks.

Follow-up:
After treatment, the patient was told how important it is to take all medicines as directed. She was also told to come back to the hospital for check-up visits. The doctors will watch for any returning symptoms.

The coughing up of blood stopped after surgery to remove part of her lung. After 3 weeks, tests showed no more tuberculosis germs. The patient responded well to treatment and is now in month 4. She was told to keep taking her medicines and come back for follow-up visits.

The patient is a 30-year-old Japanese man. He was admitted to our facility on November 8, 2016. He had symptoms of feeling overly important and being easily angered. In the past, the patient had a head injury that caused him to be unconscious for 2 weeks. He recovered after 3 months. After that, he had trouble controlling his emotions, but this got better over time. The patient passed an audition for an entertainment company at age 12. He then performed on TV shows and on stage. During high school, he studied in Australia and got tattoos on his whole back. At 21 years old, he had a child. He then worked on a motor race rescue team. Later, he switched to work at his family's company. At 29 years old, he had problems with his sister. He became distant from his family. Before coming to our hospital, the patient worked selling clothes. He was also taking lessons in Japanese classical dance and classical ballet.

The patient was acting in a confused way. He chose to enter a hospital on his own. Doctors said he was having a manic episode, which is a period of very high energy and unusual behavior. He was first given a medicine called aripiprazole. However, his symptoms kept getting worse. The patient bought an expensive Japanese sword and telescope over the phone. He also showed behavior that was sexual and not appropriate.

The patient's hospital stay was changed from his choice to required by doctors. He was moved to our hospital for more testing. After arriving, he was given a medicine called carbamazepine along with aripiprazole. After this, his feelings of being overly important and his anger went away. 9 months after leaving the hospital, in February 2017, the patient said his life was back to normal. During his stay at our hospital, the patient was slow at processing information and had trouble paying attention. These problems got better after treatment. Tests done after leaving the hospital still showed some slowness in processing and attention.

In summary, the patient came to our hospital because of a manic episode. He was treated with carbamazepine along with aripiprazole. This treatment worked well to stop his feelings of being overly important and his anger. The patient got better and said his life returned to normal after leaving our hospital.

The patient was diagnosed with a fatty growth made of certain cells called a PEComa. There were no signs of cancer.

The growth could be felt through the belly wall but did not cause pain. Blood tests showed mild low iron levels in the blood but everything else was normal.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [NAME]
Age: 69
Gender: Male

Diagnosis:
Heart attack affecting the front wall of the heart, Heart Failure

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital in September 2017 for heart bypass surgery, repair of two heart valves, and replacement of another heart valve. A special wire was placed in the heart, and the heart device was upgraded to help the heart pump better and correct dangerous heart rhythms. A heart monitoring feature was set up and ready to use starting January 2018.

Progress Notes:
In January 2018, the patient had mild heart failure symptoms and normal fluid levels in the body. Blood tests showed reduced kidney function and high levels of a hormone that shows heart stress. The heart monitor score was 8, which is at the high end of normal. On February 5th, the heart monitor sent an alert because the score went above the warning level of 16. A review of the device data showed the score had slowly risen to 17 over two weeks. The patient was called and said he had no symptoms or signs of fluid buildup. A follow-up phone call was made two weeks later. Even though the heart monitor score rose to 25, the patient still felt fine. However, he admitted to drinking more fluids and eating more salt than advised. The patient was told to cut back on fluids and salt. The heart monitor score stopped rising but did not go down. An office visit was then scheduled.

At the office visit, the patient first said he had no symptoms. But during his exercise program, he had mild trouble breathing. The doctor found swollen neck veins and mild ankle swelling. Blood tests showed worse kidney function and higher levels of the heart stress hormone. The heart monitor score was 22. The patient was slowly building up extra fluid in his body. The dose of his water pill was increased. After this change, the patient could exercise better and finished his exercise program. The heart monitor score also dropped to 0.

Follow-up:
At a follow-up visit in April, the patient had no signs of fluid buildup. Blood tests showed better kidney function and lower levels of the heart stress hormone. The patient is now in stable condition with mild heart failure symptoms. The patient has not needed to go back to the hospital for worsening heart failure.

Impression:
The heart monitor was successfully used as part of the heart failure care plan. The monitor may also help guide changes to medicine for patients at home.

Hospital Course:
The 61-year-old female patient has a history of ovarian cancer and noncancerous growths in the liver made of blood vessels. The patient was sent to the liver surgery department. When the patient arrived, doctors found several spots in the liver. These spots were first thought to be noncancerous blood vessel growths. However, doctors also found a new growth in one part of the liver. This growth had both solid and fluid-filled areas with walls inside it. A special scan showed the solid parts of this growth. The doctor who read the scan thought it might be a noncancerous cyst or a cancerous cyst in the liver.

A full body scan did not show signs that the growth was using extra sugar, which cancer cells often do. After surgery, doctors looked at the growth closely. It was soft and looked like a honeycomb. Under a microscope, doctors saw widened fluid channels and tiny blood vessels of different sizes. These were mixed with a small number of immune cells and red blood cells. All blood tests for cancer markers came back normal. These tests included checks for liver cancer and other types of cancer.

Outcome:
The patient stayed in the hospital and was watched closely. The patient had regular checkups during the stay. The patient's liver was working normally based on blood tests. There were no major problems during the hospital stay. The patient was then sent home with instructions to keep getting regular checkups.

Follow-up:
The patient's regular doctor was told to make sure the patient gets checkups and imaging tests at the right times.

target_forms_elicited: rare disease where abnormal cells build up and can damage bones
items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 45-year-old man. He came to the hospital with pain in his left side, numbness, and weakness in both legs. During the exam, the patient had weak muscles in both legs. The patient also had stronger than normal reflexes in the right knee. Tests showed that a bone tumor had caused breaks in the spine bones called T8 and T9. The tumor was also pressing on the spinal cord and causing nerve problems.

The patient had surgery to remove the damaged spine bone at T9. Doctors put in a metal cage to support the spine. They also placed screws at T8 through T10 to hold the spine steady. Lab tests of the removed tissue showed a condition called Langerhans cell histiocytosis. This is a rare disease where abnormal cells build up and can damage bones. The patient then had radiation treatment on the T8 through T10 area of the spine. After treatment, the leg weakness and numbness got much better.

The patient has been checked for almost 6 years with no sign of the tumor coming back. Discharge instructions included follow-up visits with the regular doctor. The patient should also get regular scans to make sure the bone tumor does not return.

Overall, the patient received excellent medical care from the healthcare team and responded well to treatment.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Date of Admission: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 47-year-old woman, came to the hospital with pain in both sides of her groin, not being able to urinate, and bloody discharge from her vagina. A physical exam showed a large dying tissue mass filling the entire vaginal canal. An ultrasound of the belly showed a mass in the cervix and vagina area measuring about 4.4 by 4.5 inches. The mass was coming out from inside the uterus, and the uterus looked twisted out of shape. After more tests and an MRI scan, doctors confirmed a large non-cancerous growth called a fibroid attached to the inside top of the uterus. The uterus was pulled into a V-shape because the mass was dragging on it.

Blood tests showed the patient had low red blood cell levels at 10.1 g/dL and 30.9 percent, which means mild blood loss. The patient also had high inflammation markers at 37.5 mg/L. Blood sugar and liver tests were normal. A test called CA125, which checks for certain problems, was high at 152 U/mL.

During surgery through the belly, doctors found a large growth in the uterus that had caused the uterus to turn inside out. The growth was removed by cutting into the uterus after finding where it was attached. The uterus, both fallopian tubes, and both ovaries were then removed because the patient asked for this before surgery. The removed tissue showed a very large mass with dead tissue and areas of bleeding. Lab tests on the tissue confirmed a fibroid measuring about 4.7 by 4.7 by 4 inches with large areas of dead tissue. There were no signs of cancer.

The patient left the hospital five days after surgery with no problems.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Uterus turned inside out with a non-cancerous uterine growth called a fibroid.

Discharge Condition:
Stable.

Discharge Medication:
None.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was told to follow up with her women's health doctor and regular doctor. She was told not to lift heavy things or have sex for six weeks so her body can fully heal. She was also told to watch for any signs of vaginal bleeding, pain, or fever. If any of these happen, she should call her doctor right away.

Follow-Up:
The patient was told to make an appointment with her women's health doctor and regular doctor to check on her healing.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 41
Sex: Female
Admission Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: [Redacted]
Admission Diagnosis: Suspected COVID-19 infection

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with a dry cough, trouble breathing, chest tightness, fever, chills, body aches, mild sore throat, and watery diarrhea. Tests ruled out several lung infections, but a COVID-19 test came back positive after a breathing tube was placed. A special scan of the chest showed infection in both lungs. The patient was then started on medicines through an IV to fight infection, including vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, azithromycin, and hydroxychloroquine.

Over time, her condition got worse. She developed a serious lung problem where the lungs cannot get enough oxygen into the blood. She needed stronger breathing machine settings and had to lie face down to help her breathe. Her liver showed signs of damage, and her kidneys started to fail because not enough blood was reaching her organs.

The patient was given high doses of vitamin C, zinc sulfate, and tocilizumab to control a dangerous overreaction of her immune system. Even with treatment, her condition kept getting worse. A machine was started to filter her blood because her kidneys failed. Another machine was added to put oxygen directly into her blood.

During treatment with the blood oxygen machine, the patient developed a blood clotting problem and loss of blood flow to her fingers and toes on both sides. Even though a blood test for this problem came back negative, a blood thinner called Argatroban was given because her blood cell count dropped while on another blood thinner. Even though her heart and blood pressure stayed stable, the patient died four days after starting the blood oxygen machine because her heart stopped beating.

Discharge Plan:
The patient passed away during her treatment with the blood oxygen machine. Comfort care and support were given to the family. The next of kin was told to follow up with her regular doctor for any further concerns. No further treatment or tests were scheduled.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Overview:
The 72-year-old white male came to the hospital with general weakness, worsening shortness of breath, and cough. His health history includes a blood cancer called chronic lymphatic leukemia, high blood pressure, several skin cancers on the scalp, and heavy alcohol use. His regular medicines are atorvastatin, irbesartan, and propranolol.

Hospital Course:
During the physical exam, the patient's blood pressure was 109/76 mmHg. His heart rate was 167 beats per minute and not steady. He was breathing 28 times per minute. Blood tests showed signs of infection and inflammation. The tests also showed high levels of white blood cells, high lactic acid, high blood sugar, slightly high liver test results, blood clotting problems, and a mild form of low red blood cells. A test of blood oxygen levels showed low oxygen and low carbon dioxide. A chest X-ray looked normal.

The patient was first diagnosed with a lung infection caught outside the hospital. He was given antibiotics through an IV and a blood thinner for an irregular heartbeat. Within a few hours, the patient's heart stopped beating. He was moved to intensive care and put on a breathing machine. Doctors made a small opening in his throat to help him breathe. After he no longer needed the breathing machine, he was moved to a regular hospital room.

Doctors took a fluid sample from the lungs. The sample tested positive for a virus called herpes simplex virus type 1. A sample from the breathing tube also tested positive for this virus. The lung fluid sample also showed growth of a yeast called Candida albicans. The patient received antiviral medicine for 14 days and antibiotics for 10 days. This treatment helped lower the infection and inflammation levels in the blood.

The patient was sent home after 29 days. He was successfully taken off the breathing machine.

Advised Follow-up:
The patient was told to see his regular doctor to check on his blood cancer, high blood pressure, and skin cancers on the scalp. The patient was also told to get help for his heavy alcohol use.

Discharge Medications:
The patient was not given any medicines to take home at this time.

Primary Diagnosis:
A lung infection caught outside the hospital that led to severe lung damage, very low oxygen levels, a new irregular heartbeat, and the heart stopping.

Secondary Diagnosis:
Blood cancer called chronic lymphatic leukemia, high blood pressure, several skin cancers on the scalp, high blood sugar, slightly high liver test results, blood clotting problems, and mild low red blood cells.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 7-year-old female

Admission Dates: [Date of admission] to [Date of discharge]

Diagnosis/Problem: A rare disease where the body's immune system causes swelling and scarring in the tissue that holds the intestines in place

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 7-year-old female, was admitted after one month of cramping belly pain, throwing up, loose stools, and fever. Three years earlier, she was told she had a lung infection that spread to her belly. She took medicine for 9 months but did not get better. She came back to the hospital with the same problems. Doctors then thought she had Crohn's disease based on a special X-ray scan of her belly. She took steroids and other medicines to calm her immune system, but she still did not improve. No one in her family has had gut problems or diseases where the body attacks itself. She had no night sweats, skin rashes, joint pain, or recent trips to other places. When she came to the hospital, her exam showed she was smaller than expected for her age. Blood tests showed normal red blood cells, white blood cells, and cells that help blood clot. Her body salts, blood clotting, and liver were all working normally. She had high levels of a marker that shows swelling in the body. She had low levels of a protein that keeps fluid in the blood. Three types of her immune proteins were normal, but one type called IgG4 was too high. Doctors used a camera to look inside her food pipe, stomach, and large intestine. The lining looked normal with no sores. A special X-ray scan of her belly showed many swollen glands and a lot of swelling and irritation in the tissue near the end of her small intestine.

Doctors did surgery to look inside her belly because they thought she might have cancer of the immune system based on the scan. During surgery, they found that her organs were stuck together inside her belly. They also found swollen glands and swelling in the fatty tissue that covers the intestines. They took small tissue samples from the glands and the lining inside her belly. The samples showed scarring around the glands and clusters of immune cells. A special test using markers for immune proteins showed that most of the immune cells were making too much IgG4 protein. Doctors determined she had a rare disease where the body makes too much IgG4 protein. This causes swelling and scarring in the tissue that holds the intestines. She was given four medicines: one to reduce swelling, one to protect her stomach, one steroid, and one to calm her immune system.

At 6 months after starting treatment, she felt completely well. The mass in her belly tissue got smaller. Her blood tests stayed normal. She did develop fluid around her heart, but it got better with a higher dose of steroid medicine. The patient now takes a low dose of steroid medicine each day. She has had no return of her symptoms during the 24 months since treatment started.

items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary
Patient: 39-year-old male

Medical History:
The patient had a history of hay fever. He reported many episodes of dizziness and patches of hives, with chest tightness that happened either with or shortly after exercise over the previous 3 months. Over time, the episodes had become more frequent and severe and required several treatments to relieve his symptoms. The patient was diagnosed with a condition that causes swelling in the food pipe due to a type of white blood cell. This was confirmed through a small tissue sample.

Hospital Course:
The patient was given several medications to treat his throat and chest tightness with exercise, but they did not completely resolve his symptoms. He later tried to avoid wheat and all food for up to 12 hours before exercise but to no avail.

To manage his condition, the patient chose to start a trial of omalizumab, which was given in doses of 300 mg every 2 weeks. No food restrictions were given during this time. The patient reported major improvement, and he was able to exercise three times a week without any symptoms. He had only one episode of mild hives, but it happened when he had missed one of his omalizumab injections. The patient continued to exercise normally, reporting any symptoms that he had and was followed up monthly.

The patient later experienced episodes of hives, greatly increased chest tightness, and swelling around the eyes after at least 15 minutes of exercise. He ultimately had an episode of a severe allergic reaction with hives, difficulty breathing, and facial swelling and was admitted to the emergency room, where he received several treatments to relieve his symptoms. After this episode, omalizumab was restarted at the same doses and intervals.

Follow-up and Outcome:
The patient continued on omalizumab with no further episodes of severe allergic reactions and no restrictions on his activity level. He is expected to continue being followed up monthly and continue exercising normally.

Diagnostic Findings:

Blood tests showed a high white blood cell count when the patient arrived. This went back to normal during her stay. Kidney tests were normal. Doctors from different areas worked together to care for the patient. These included general medicine, eye doctors, joint doctors, and infection doctors. She left the hospital in good condition.

items.clean_ref:
Patient: 37-year-old African-American female with sickle cell disease (a blood disorder)

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the clinic with sudden vision loss in her right eye. During the exam, she could only see hand movements with her right eye. Her left eye had normal 20/20 vision. Her pupils responded normally to light. There was heavy bleeding inside her right eye that blocked the doctor's view of the back of the eye. The patient also had some changes to the nerve and blood vessels at the back of her eye.

Treatment and Management:
The patient had surgery on her right eye to remove the blood and treat the bleeding. The doctor used a small camera and laser during the surgery. Some scar tissue was carefully cut away. Other scar tissue was left alone because it was stuck tightly to important blood vessels.

Follow-up:
At the 1-month follow-up visit, the patient reported sudden painless vision loss in her left eye 2 days before. Her right eye vision had improved to 20/100. Her left eye vision was 20/50. Her pupils still responded normally. The doctor looked at the back of her left eye and saw pale patches near the center. This meant some small blood vessels had become blocked. A scan done a few weeks later showed some leftover scar tissue in her right eye. The scan of her left eye showed damage to the inner layers from the blocked blood vessels.

Recommendations:
The doctor offered a special dye test to confirm what was wrong, but the patient said no. The patient should continue to be checked regularly to make sure her condition is managed well.

A rare cancer that started in the blood vessels of the lungs and spread to other areas

The patient came to the hospital with worsening trouble breathing and coughing up blood. A special scan of the lungs showed a blockage in an artery in the right upper lung. The patient was treated for a blood clot in the lungs with blood-thinning medicines. However, the breathing problems got worse, so the patient was moved to our hospital.

A tissue sample taken during this surgery showed cancer cells. This confirmed a rare cancer that started in the blood vessels of the lungs.

Discharge Summary:

This is a summary of the medical care for a 3-month-old boy who came in with a seizure that affected part of his brain. A head scan showed bleeding inside the brain. The bleeding was caused by a burst blood vessel bulge near the front of the brain. This bulge was very large and had formed a blood clot on its own. Another scan and a test to look at blood vessels confirmed a growth above a bone at the base of the skull. The growth was about one inch wide and matched a large blood vessel bulge. The patient was moved to a special care unit for very sick children. There he was given medicine to stop seizures, medicine to reduce brain swelling, and medicine for pain and sleep. He was also placed on a breathing machine. A small tube was placed to drain fluid from the brain. A test to look at the brain's blood vessels was done. It confirmed that a blood clot had blocked the blood vessel bulge. A tube was placed to move extra fluid from the brain to the belly area. This helped treat fluid buildup in the brain. The child was seen by doctors who specialize in children's brain and nerve problems. He also saw surgeons who operate on children's brains. He got much better and healed without any problems. Follow-up tests to look at blood vessels were done over five years. These tests showed that blood did not start flowing again through the blood vessel bulge. The patient's brain and nerves are working normally. He has no limits on his activities. He has not had any more seizures.

Stroke in the left side of the brain, moving blood clot on the replacement heart valve

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital after having a stroke in the left side of her brain. She also had a moving blood clot on her replacement heart valve. Doctors gave her a blood thinner called heparin to stop more clots and shrink the existing one. The blood clot did not get smaller. Blood tests were done. Doctors found out the patient has a condition where the blood clots too easily. This condition is called antiphospholipid syndrome.

Doctors did surgery to remove the blood clot from the heart valve. The patient was given medicine through a vein to make her sleep during surgery. A heart-lung machine was used to pump blood during the operation. The patient received blood thinning medicine during surgery. After surgery, the patient went to the intensive care unit. She was bleeding too much, so doctors gave her medicine called protamine to help stop the bleeding.

After surgery, blood tests showed the blood was too thin. Doctors gave more protamine to control the bleeding. The patient was given a blood thinner pill called warfarin to prevent future clots. The patient left the hospital 9 days after surgery.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Stroke in the left side of the brain, moving blood clot on replacement heart valve, a condition that causes blood to clot too easily called antiphospholipid syndrome

Stable

The patient should keep taking warfarin to prevent blood clots.

The patient came to the hospital for a tumor on the head of the pancreas. This was found using a scan that takes pictures of the inside of the body. This narrowing was caused by hardened buildup in the blood vessel walls. Doctors used small balloons to open up the narrowed blood vessel two times before surgery. This helped improve blood flow. The patient then received four rounds of cancer-fighting drugs called gemcitabine and paclitaxel. These drugs were given before surgery to help shrink the tumor.
